USA.story:
In 1974, in the Diocese of Lafayette, Louisiana, the bishop made Fr Gilbert Gauthe chaplain to a Boy Scout troop, although there were already allegations that he had abused altar boys. In 1976 Gauthe was sent for therapy and then returned to work. He later admitted abusing 37 children between 1972 and 1983. In October 1985 he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 20 years, and the diocese paid more than $20 million. It was the first clergy abuse prosecution in the country to be widely publicised.

The same steps repeated elsewhere. In Stockton, California, Bishop Roger Mahony knew of concerns about Fr Oliver O'Grady by 1980; after police declined to charge him in 1984, Mahony moved him to another parish and later made him pastor. O'Grady was convicted in 1993. In 2018 a Pennsylvania grand jury named 301 priests and at least 1,000 child victims across six dioceses over about 70 years, found that bishops had moved abusers, and noted that most of the crimes were too old to prosecute. No national inquiry into institutional abuse was found in the sources; the investigations have been run by state attorneys general and grand juries, or commissioned by the church, like the bishops' study that in 2004 counted 10,667 allegations against 4,392 clergy.

People with money and fame waited inside the same gap. Maria Farmer reported Jeffrey Epstein to the FBI in 1996 with no known action. After a 2005 Palm Beach police investigation, a 2007 federal non-prosecution agreement ended the federal case, and he served 13 months in a county stockade on a state plea. Federal sex-trafficking charges came in July 2019, after a Miami Herald series. He died in his cell on 10 August 2019; the Justice Department's inspector general later found guards had skipped checks and falsified records. Ghislaine Maxwell was convicted of sex trafficking of a minor in 2021 and sentenced to 20 years. Athletes complained about the gymnastics doctor Larry Nassar from 1997; the FBI was told in July 2015 and did not act, and at least 70 more athletes were abused before his arrest.

When survivors finally came forward, the legal deadline to sue, called a statute of limitations, had often passed. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million lobbying in eight northeastern states from 2011 to 2018, and at least 41 dioceses and orders, the Boy Scouts and USA Gymnastics filed for bankruptcy. In Milwaukee, $57 million was moved into a cemetery trust, out of victims' reach.

The United States is also the largest receiver of children on this map: 109,242 from South Korea between 1953 and 2008, and 87,704 from China, 60,266 from Russia and 32,863 from Guatemala between 1994 and 2014. At home, the state itself removed Native children through boarding schools and the Indian Adoption Project (1958 to 1967). In 2025, 49,021 web addresses with abuse material traced to US servers, 16% of the total the Internet Watch Foundation removed.

False stories took attention away from all of this: the McMartin preschool trials ended without a conviction, and the 'Pizzagate' claim of a child-trafficking ring at a Washington pizzeria was false.

For a novice, the American record shows that most cases came out through grand juries, journalists and lawsuits, not through the institutions that first heard the complaints. When you read about a case, ask who was told first, in what year, and what they did next.

PHL.story:
In 1992 the mayor of Manila, Alfredo Lim, closed the Ermita district, where the sex industry had been concentrated. Many of the businesses moved north to Angeles City. The US Clark Air Base there had closed the same year, and the bars found new customers among sex tourists. The US government's 2025 trafficking report still names Angeles City, Boracay, Olongapo, Puerto Galera and Surigao as places where sex trafficking often happens. It says most foreign offenders come from Australia, Japan, New Zealand, the UK and the US, that many are already convicted or charged sex offenders at home, and that corruption and official complicity remain significant concerns.

As police pressure grew on the bars, the abuse moved indoors and online. One study found that child sex trafficking in establishments fell 79% to 86% in targeted cities between 2006 and 2016, while Philippine internet addresses used for child sexual exploitation grew more than twelvefold per month from 2014 to 2017. In the new form, a buyer abroad pays a family member or neighbour to abuse a child on a webcam while he watches and gives instructions. One Australian man did this over Skype for nearly five years, paying the children's mother; the children were two and seven when it began. Another Australian, Peter Scully, moved to Cagayan de Oro in 2011 and sold videos of abuse to customers abroad. A tip from Dutch police led to his arrest in 2015; he was sentenced to life in 2018 and a further 129 years in 2022.

The money trail runs through ordinary banks. Australia's Westpac agreed a A$1.3 billion penalty in 2020 for breaking money-laundering law, including failures over payments that could be linked to child exploitation. In 2024 Europol investigators went through more than 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 sellers in the Philippines, producing leads to 197 buyers in 24 countries. In 2017, 64% of the cases handled by the Philippine anti-trafficking unit began with a referral from foreign police. International Justice Mission estimates that 1 in every 100 Filipino children was a victim of online sexual exploitation in 2022.

Powerful people at home are another part of the story. The preacher Apollo Quiboloy, close to former President Rodrigo Duterte, was charged with sex trafficking in the United States in November 2021, refused to cooperate with Philippine inquiries, and faced a Senate arrest warrant in March 2024. The Catholic bishops apologised in 2002 and said about 200 of 7,000 priests had committed sexual misconduct over two decades, but the country has held no national inquiry. From 2003 to 2022, 7,853 Filipino children were sent abroad for adoption.

For a novice, the Philippines shows that closing a red-light district does not end the demand; it moves the abuse into homes and onto screens. The buyers and the payments mostly come from wealthy countries, so it is worth asking what those countries' police and banks are doing.

CHL.story:
In 1959, in Siegburg, West Germany, authorities issued a warrant for Paul Schäfer for abusing two boys. He fled, and in January 1961 settled in southern Chile with a small group of followers, where he founded a commune called Colonia Dignidad. The colony ran a free school and clinic and recruited children from local farms. In 1966 a teenager who escaped took refuge at the West German embassy; the embassy sent a delegation and said it found no evidence, and German diplomats went on praising it as a 'model colony'. Escapees' accounts in the 1960s were rejected by politicians because of the colony's ties to the men preparing the 1973 coup. Under the Pinochet dictatorship, Chilean officials believe the colony was used by the secret police, DINA, to torture opponents.

An investigation opened only after Chilean mothers complained in 1997. Schäfer disappeared that May and hid in Argentina until he was found in March 2005. In May 2006 a Chilean court sentenced him to 20 years for sexually abusing 25 children; he died in prison in 2010. The colony's doctor, Hartmut Hopp, was convicted in 2011 of helping the abuse, then fled to Germany, where prosecutors dropped their own investigation in 2019. Germany's foreign minister admitted in 2016 that diplomats had 'at best looked away' for decades.

Inside the church, parishioners reported Fr Fernando Karadima to Archbishop Fresno in 1984. A church investigation in 2004 and 2005 found the complaints credible, and Cardinal Errázuriz shelved it. The Vatican found Karadima guilty in 2011, but in 2015 one of his protégés, Juan Barros, was made bishop of Osorno. After a 2,300-page Vatican report in 2018, every bishop in Chile offered to resign. In 2010 the Marist Brothers moved Brother Abel Pérez to Peru after he confessed to abusing minors. In July 2019 Chile removed the legal time limit for prosecuting child sexual abuse.

The state itself also harmed children. Babies were taken from poor mothers, some told their child had died, and sent for adoption to the United States and Europe; a judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 into about 8,000 adoptions abroad from 1970 to 1999, and as of 2023 nobody had been brought to justice. In state child protection, SENAME, the UN found sexual abuse and torture in residences and 210 deaths between 2005 and 2016. A 2013 judicial audit found a sexual exploitation network organised by carers in one Arica home, where 24 girls left the home and came back drugged at dawn; the report was held back until journalists published it.

For a novice, Chile shows how an abuser can be protected when he is useful to people in power, here a dictatorship and a foreign embassy. When a closed community or institution has friends in government, ask who inspected it and what they reported.

ROU.story:
In 1966 Romania's Decree 770 banned abortion. Many of the children born in the years that followed were left in state orphanages and institutions for disabled children, where they suffered neglect, sedation, and physical and sexual abuse; at the Siret children's psychiatric hospital, physical and sexual abuse was reported to be common. When Ceaușescu fell in 1989, television showed about 100,000 children in orphanages, and foreign families came to adopt. Private agencies charged €7,500 to €25,000 per child, and the system, in the words of the German broadcaster DW, 'quickly became awash in corruption'.

Romania put adoptions on hold in July 1990, halted them in June 1991 and outlawed baby selling that August. In 2001 a government commission found that money had been siphoned off by middlemen and officials, and a temporary ban followed. Adoptions still went out in 2002: 458 that year, 257 of them to the United States. In June 2004, under pressure from the European Union, Romania banned foreign adoption except by grandparents. Between 1994 and 2008, 5,285 Romanian children were adopted into the United States.

The risk to children in state care did not end with the ban. The 2025 US trafficking report says girls in government-run homes, particularly homes for people with disabilities, are at risk of sex trafficking, and that alleged complicity and negligence by government staff in those cases remains a concern. One method is called 'loverboy': a man poses as a boyfriend and then sells the girl. In September 2020 Romanian and British investigators arrested 21 members of a group active since 2009 that exploited Romanian girls in prostitution until they turned 18, then moved them to the UK, Ireland and Germany. In the 1990s and early 2000s, girls from Romania were also among those trafficked into post-war Bosnia and Kosovo, where foreign peacekeepers and contractors were among the buyers.

Romania now plays a part online as well. In 2025 it hosted 21,188 web addresses removed by the Internet Watch Foundation, 7% of the total, and 14% of the abuse material confirmed by the INHOPE hotline network. In 2015 a 17-year-old in Coalisland, Northern Ireland, took his own life after a man posing as a girl blackmailed him with intimate images; a 31-year-old Romanian was sentenced in Timișoara in 2017 to four years.

For a novice, Romania shows that children in large state institutions are the easiest to sell, first through adoption agencies and later through traffickers. When a country closes one route, ask whether the children in its care homes are any safer, or only being moved by a different method.

CAF.story:
Between December 2013 and June 2014, at the camp for displaced people at Bangui's M'Poko airport, six boys aged 9 to 13 told UN staff that French soldiers had sexually abused them in exchange for food rations. The soldiers belonged to Operation Sangaris, a French force not under UN command. The UN did not pass its internal report to French authorities. A UN official, Anders Kompass, passed it on himself; he was suspended, and resigned in 2016 in protest at the lack of punishment. Paris prosecutors opened an inquiry in July 2014 that grew to cover accusations from fifteen children. In January 2018 French judges dismissed the case for lack of sufficient charges, citing inconsistencies in testimony. The prosecutor said it could not be affirmed that no abuse had been committed. No soldier was charged.

UN peacekeepers came next. A peacekeeper is tried, if at all, by the courts of the country that sent them, not by the country where the abuse happened. In Dékoa, allegations against soldiers from Gabon and Burundi led to interviews with some 136 alleged victims, 48% of all victims the UN recorded in 2016. Press accounts said 41 troops were identified and sent home without charges. Human Rights Watch documented eight cases near Bambari airport in late 2015, including a 14-year-old girl who said she was gang-raped, when a Republic of Congo contingent guarded the airport. The UN listed 17 allegations against soldiers from DR Congo, with 15 child victims; that battalion left in January 2016. In September 2021 the UN sent home all of Gabon's roughly 450 soldiers after new allegations.

The armed groups fighting inside the country also take children. From 2008 the Lord's Resistance Army, which had abducted tens of thousands of children in northern Uganda, moved into DR Congo, South Sudan and the Central African Republic and abducted thousands more. In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 114 girls in the country: 58 by armed groups of the CPC coalition, and 35 by government and pro-government forces, including 9 by the Wagner-linked Azande group. It verified the abduction of 141 children. No representative surveys of online abuse exist for West and Central Africa, so that side of the picture is not counted at all.

For a novice, the Central African Republic shows that the people sent to protect children can abuse them, and that sending them home usually ends the matter. When you read that a unit was 'repatriated', ask whether any court in its home country ever tried anyone.

HTI.story:
From 2004 to 2007, soldiers from Sri Lanka served in Haiti as part of the UN peacekeeping mission, MINUSTAH. A UN oversight office later concluded that their sexual exploitation and abuse of children 'were frequent and occurred usually at night, and at virtually every location where the contingent personnel were deployed', and said the charges should include statutory rape, meaning sex with a child below the legal age of consent. An Associated Press investigation in 2017 found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had exploited at least nine children in a sex ring. Under UN rules, peacekeepers can only be tried by their own country. In November 2007, 114 members of the contingent were accused and 108 were sent home. Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts 'consensual', nobody was jailed, and in 2016 Sri Lanka made a single goodwill payment to one victim.

The 2010 earthquake brought aid workers. Oxfam GB's own 2011 investigation found staff in Haiti had used prostitutes, some alleged to be underage. Staff, including the country director, were allowed to resign. A British regulator found in 2019 that Oxfam had not fully investigated a July 2011 email alleging that its employees were sexually abusing minors, and had not reported it to the regulator or police; by then it was no longer possible to say for certain whether minors had been involved.

The earthquake also sped up the movement of children out of the country. On 29 January 2010, ten American Baptist missionaries were stopped trying to take 33 children across the border to the Dominican Republic without proper papers. The kidnapping charges were dropped, and the organiser, Laura Silsby, was convicted only of arranging illegal travel. About 1,090 children were brought to the US under emergency permission that year. Three years earlier, a Haitian centre had been forced to return 47 children held for international adoption after it misled parents with payments. Between 2003 and 2022, 13,986 Haitian children were sent abroad for adoption. A study by the charity Lumos found that 92% of orphanage funders were from the US and 90% were faith-based, and that the donations themselves drive new orphanages to open, some purely for profit, which then recruit children from their families.

Today the main threat comes from armed gangs. The UN verified sexual violence against 566 children in Haiti in 2024, up from 41 girls in 2023; 411 cases were attributed to the Viv Ansanm gang coalition. Many children also live as restavek, sent to work unpaid as servants in other families' homes, where the 2025 US trafficking report says they are often physically abused and more at risk of sexual exploitation.

For a novice, Haiti shows how a disaster draws in outsiders, from soldiers to charities to adopters, and how each group answers mainly to its own home country. When money flows into orphanages, ask whether the children there actually have no parents.

ARG.story:
On 17 April 1977, in a secret detention centre known as 'La Escuelita' in Bahía Blanca, a woman whose family had been kidnapped in Cutral Có, Neuquén, gave birth to a boy. Under Argentina's military dictatorship (1976 to 1983), babies born to detained or disappeared mothers were taken and handed to military families and allies of the regime, who registered them as their own children. Many grew up not knowing they had been adopted. That boy was identified as an adult in July 2025, the 140th of about 500 such children found by the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo, a group of grandmothers who began searching in 1977. Their work led to Argentina's National Bank of Genetic Data, which matches DNA from families to people who suspect they were taken.

The courts caught up decades later. On 5 July 2012 a Buenos Aires federal tribunal found that the junta had run a 'systematic plan' to take these children. Former dictator Jorge Videla was sentenced to 50 years and the last dictator, Reynaldo Bignone, to 15 years. The same practice crossed borders: a pregnant 19-year-old detained in Buenos Aires in 1976 was moved secretly to Montevideo, and her baby was raised by a Uruguayan police officer's family for 23 years.

Trafficking for sex has its own record. In 2002, 23-year-old Marita Verón disappeared in Tucumán, allegedly abducted into forced prostitution. In December 2012 a court acquitted all 13 defendants, which set off national protests. A year later Tucumán's Supreme Court reversed the verdict and found 10 of them guilty. Campaigners said police were often paid to protect brothel rings, and the network the case exposed also trafficked minors. Bolivian women and girls are trafficked into Argentina for sex.

The church moved people in both directions. Fr Nicola Corradi was accused at the Provolo school for deaf children in Verona, Italy, in 2009 and then worked at the order's school in Mendoza, where he was arrested in 2016 and sentenced in 2019 to 42 years for abusing deaf children. Bishop Gustavo Zanchetta resigned from Orán in 2017 amid complaints from clergy and was given a post at the Vatican; he was convicted in Argentina in 2022 of abusing two adult seminarians. The Chilean colony leader Paul Schäfer hid in Argentina from 1997 until he was found in 2005.

For a novice, Argentina shows that a government can take children as policy, and that it took grandmothers searching from 1977, a DNA database and a court verdict in 2012 to prove it. When a state hides where children came from, ask who kept the records and who can open them.

NOR.story:
Norway's part in this map is mainly that of a receiving country. Between 1955 and 2008, 6,295 South Korean children were sent to Norway for adoption, part of about 163,898 sent abroad from South Korea in that period. In 1974 and 1975, when South Korea tried to stop sending children, Scandinavian diplomats pressed it to continue.

In March 2025, South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported on petitions from 367 adoptees sent to 11 countries between 1964 and 1999. It found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. Agencies had sent set numbers of children each month to meet demand from foreign agencies, registered children who had known parents as orphans, failed to get proper consent and did not check adoptive parents. When a child died before departure, another child's identity was sometimes swapped in. The commission said the Korean state had treated overseas adoption as a cheap substitute for welfare at home. South Korea's president apologised in October 2025.

Norway began to look at its own side in 2023, when it opened an investigation into whether illegal or unethical practices occurred in intercountry adoptions and whether Norwegian officials failed to control them. The foreign ministry said in 2024 that it was 'aware of serious findings'. In September 2025 a Korean-born adoptee gave notice that she would sue the Norwegian state, alleging her adoption was illegal; that claim has not been tested in court.

A separate thread runs through the Epstein files. After the US Justice Department released Epstein documents in 2026, Norway's economic-crime agency investigated former prime minister Thorbjørn Jagland over whether he received gifts, travel and loans in connection with his position. In February 2026 his lawyers said he had been charged with aggravated corruption. He denies the charges. It is a corruption case, not an abuse charge, and it is recorded here only for the reach of Epstein's contacts into politics.

For a novice, Norway shows that a receiving country can be part of an adoption system that went wrong, through demand and diplomatic pressure, without any abuse happening on its soil. When a country adopted many children from abroad, ask whether it has checked how those children were obtained.

BLR.story:
On 30 July 2003, in a Paris hotel, US agents arrested two men from Minsk: Yahor Zalatarou, president of a company called Regpay, and its marketing director, Alexei Buchnev. The next day Regpay's technical administrator, Aliaksandr Boika, was arrested in Tarragona, Spain. Regpay had processed paid memberships to about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it ran itself, for thousands of subscribers around the world. Customers paid by credit card, the payments were routed through Latvian banks, and a Florida company, Connections, helped launder the money. All three men pleaded guilty in New Jersey. In 2006 Zalatarou and Boika were each sentenced to 25 years and Buchnev to 40 months; Connections' chief executive pleaded guilty to money laundering, and hundreds of subscribers were arrested in the US and other countries. The case showed that abuse material could be run as a business with ordinary card payments.

Belarus also appears in the record of children moved by governments. After Russia's full invasion of Ukraine in 2022, children from occupied Ukraine were brought to Belarus; about 2,100 were transferred in 2022 and 2023. In July 2023 the head of the Belarus Red Cross said they had come for 'health improvement' and that this would continue. In March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Russia's children's commissioner, Maria Lvova-Belova, over the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children. Both are charged, not tried. The map also links Belarus to an older case: Nazi Germany's kidnapping of children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, for which 13 SS officials were convicted at Nuremberg in 1948.

For a novice, Belarus shows two kinds of movement: money flowing in to pay for abuse online, and children carried across a border during a war under the label of a health trip. When children are moved out of a war zone, ask who is recording their names and how they will get home.

SYR.story:
On 3 August 2014, Islamic State fighters attacked Sinjar, in northern Iraq, and captured thousands of Yazidis. They moved them in buses and trucks to holding sites in Tal Afar and Mosul, and then took women and girls across the border to Raqqa in Syria. There, girls as young as nine were sold at market and held as sexual slaves, and boys were forced into training camps. In June 2016 the UN commission investigating Syria found that Islamic State had committed genocide. At that time more than 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, mostly in Syria, and thousands remain missing.

The war pushed Syrian girls into danger in neighbouring countries too. In March 2016 Lebanese security forces freed as many as 75 Syrian women from two brothels, Chez Maurice and Silver-B, in Jounieh, and over a dozen people were charged with sex trafficking. The same premises had been raided in 2011, when a 17-year-old Syrian girl was found trapped there; the brothel closed for about three months and then reopened. A survivor said one trafficker claimed he had 'bought the state'. In Türkiye and Jordan, the 2025 US trafficking report says Syrian refugee girls are married off in unofficial religious ceremonies and then exploited for labour and sex.

Inside Syria the UN still verifies new cases. In 2024 it confirmed the abduction of 14 children, 9 of them girls, by the Patriotic Revolutionary Youth Movement, Syrian government forces and the Kurdish YPG/YPJ, often to recruit them as fighters. What is not counted is just as large: there is no representative survey of online child sexual abuse anywhere in the Middle East and North Africa, so nobody knows how many Syrian children are abused that way.

For a novice, Syria shows how war moves children twice: first into the hands of armed groups, then across borders as refugees, where poverty and unofficial marriages expose them again. When a brothel that held a child reopens after three months, ask who allowed it.

DNK.story:
In May 1951, Danish authorities and Save the Children Denmark asked teachers and priests in Greenland, then a Danish colony, to pick out children aged six to ten. Twenty-two Inuit children were sent to foster families in Denmark to be raised as 'little Danes', although many of their families were reluctant. About a year and a half later, 16 of them were sent back to Greenland. They were not returned to their families but placed in a children's home built by the Danish Red Cross, and many never lived with their parents again. Six were adopted in Denmark. A 2020 report found that half of the children later had mental health problems. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised in December 2020, and in March 2022, after legal action, the six survivors were each awarded 250,000 kroner.

Denmark was also a large receiver of children from abroad. Between 1965 and 2008, 9,297 South Korean children were sent to Denmark for adoption. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found that agencies had sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign demand and had registered children with known parents as orphans. Sri Lankan children were adopted into Denmark in the 1980s, during what the sources call the 'baby-farm' period. In March 2016 Denmark suspended adoptions from Ethiopia, where orphan papers had been issued for children whose parents were alive. In 2024 Denmark's only intercountry adoption agency, DIA, said it was shutting down.

For a novice, Denmark shows that removing children can be official policy in a democracy, carried out by charities and presented as help. When a government says it is giving children a better life somewhere else, ask whether the families agreed and whether the children were ever returned to them.

PAK.story:
In August 2015, people learned what had been happening for years in Hussain Khanwala, a village in Kasur district, Punjab. A local gang had filmed the sexual abuse of at least 280 children between 2006 and 2014 and then blackmailed their parents, threatening to release the videos. Parents had asked the police for help, and the police had not acted. Arrests came only after relatives clashed with the authorities on 8 August 2015 and the media took notice. The Punjab law minister called the reports a land dispute. Police and a local provincial assembly member, Malik Ahmad Saeed Khan, were alleged to have tried to cover the case up; those claims were not verified. In 2016 an anti-terrorism court in Lahore sentenced two men to life imprisonment, and 12 other accused men were acquitted.

Religious schools show a similar pattern. Pakistan has more than 22,000 registered madrassas, Islamic seminaries, with at least 2 million pupils. An Associated Press investigation in 2017 found that sexual abuse by clerics in them was widespread and seldom prosecuted. Police are often paid not to register cases, and Pakistani law allows a victim's family to 'forgive' an offender, often for money. In one case a teacher confessed to abusing a 9-year-old and was freed after the mother forgave him for $300. Police told AP that clerics are almost never convicted, and a follow-up investigation in 2020 found the same pattern.

Girls are also sent out of the country. In 2018 and 2019, brokers sold 629 poor Pakistani girls and women, many of them Christian, to Chinese men as brides. Bangladeshi girls are trafficked into Pakistan for sex. And there is no representative survey of online child sexual abuse anywhere in South Asia, so that part of the picture is not counted at all.

For a novice, Pakistan shows how a case can be closed before it begins: a police station that will not write down the complaint, or a family paid to forgive. When you see very few convictions, ask whether that reflects few crimes or a system that keeps complaints from being recorded.

BGD.story:
Near Cox's Bazar, in southeastern Bangladesh, more than one million Rohingya refugees live in 33 camps. In neighbouring Myanmar, a UN fact-finding mission found that hundreds of Rohingya women and girls were raped by the army during the 2017 'clearance operations', 80% of the confirmed cases being gang rapes. In the camps they face a new risk. The 2025 US trafficking report says tourists near Cox's Bazar have increased demand for sexual exploitation, including of Rohingya girls, and it describes corrupt policing in the camps.

Bangladeshi girls are also taken out of the country. The same report says traffickers exploit Bangladeshi women and girls for sex in India, Pakistan and the Gulf states, and observers estimate that children are 40% of the Bangladeshis trafficked for sex abroad. Corruption and official complicity are named as significant concerns. Courts convicted 103 traffickers in the latest year, down from 407 the year before.

An older thread runs through adoption. In 2021 a Dutch commission led by Tjibbe Joustra found 'serious violations' in adoptions from several countries, including Bangladesh, between 1967 and the late 1990s, and concluded that the Dutch government had known for years and failed to step in. The Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption on 8 February 2021. No representative survey of online child sexual abuse exists for South Asia, so how many Bangladeshi children are abused that way is unknown.

For a novice, Bangladesh shows how refugee camps and poverty create the conditions traffickers use, while the number of traffickers convicted fell from 407 to 103 in a year. When a country's numbers fall, ask whether the crime fell or the police and courts did less.

SOM.story:
In May 2013, near Baidoa in southern Somalia, a 12-year-old girl was allegedly raped by a Ugandan soldier serving with the African Union force, AMISOM. The force had been sent to fight the armed group Al-Shabaab and protect civilians. In September 2014 Human Rights Watch published a report based on 50 interviews, including 21 survivors. It documented 10 incidents of rape and sexual assault and 14 cases of sexual exploitation by AMISOM soldiers, mainly Ugandans at and around the force's headquarters and Burundians at their base in Mogadishu. Four of the rapes and one sexual assault involved girls under 18. Many of the victims had gone to the bases to ask for medicine or aid, one of them for her sick baby. Interpreters arranged the soldiers' access to them, and some women and girls were pressed into sex in exchange for money, food and medicine.

The armed groups the force was fighting take children in far larger numbers. In 2024 the UN verified the abduction of 887 children in Somalia, 850 of them by Al-Shabaab, mostly to make them fighters. It verified sexual violence against 267 children, 265 of them girls. Al-Shabaab was responsible for 120 cases, unidentified attackers for 110, Somali government security forces for 14, and Ethiopia's Liyu Police for 7. The UN Secretary-General noted a fivefold increase in gang rapes.

For a novice, Somalia shows that a child can be at risk both from an armed group and from the soldiers sent to fight it, and that hunger and need for medicine are what bring children within reach. When a foreign force protects a place, ask who investigates its soldiers and in which country they would be tried.

BFA.story:
Burkina Faso's record on this map comes mostly from the UN's yearly count of violations against children in war. In 2024 the UN verified the abduction of 309 children in the country. The armed group JNIM took 157, the Islamic State affiliate ISGS took 80, unidentified attackers 47, and 25 were taken by the state's own Defence and Security Forces and their civilian auxiliaries, the Volunteers for the Defence of the Homeland (VDP). The UN also verified the rape of four girls that year, two of them by the VDP. In 2022 it had verified the rape of 16 girls, 2 by the Defence and Security Forces.

Children also move across Burkina Faso's borders. The 2025 US trafficking report says Nigerian networks, some linked to Nigerian cult groups, move women and girls to mining areas in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire for sexual exploitation. In 2019 Nigerian police raided a building in Kaduna presented as an Islamic school and freed more than 300 captives; they said some had been brought from Burkina Faso, Mali and Ghana.

What is missing is any count of abuse outside the war. There is no representative survey of online child sexual abuse for West and Central Africa, so these numbers cover only what UN monitors could confirm in a conflict zone.

For a novice, Burkina Faso shows that verified numbers are a floor: each case had to be confirmed by monitors working in a war. When a government's own auxiliaries appear on the list of abductors, ask who would investigate them.

GMB.story:
Along the Senegambia Strip, the main tourist area on the coast of The Gambia, European visitors have long been a large part of the economy. The 2025 US trafficking report says some of them, primarily from the UK, reportedly travel there to exploit children, and that organised networks use European and Gambian travel agencies to promote the country as a destination for it. Women and girls from other West African countries, especially Nigeria, are recruited with offers of tourism jobs and then sexually exploited.

The Gambia tried to close this down by law. Its Tourism Offences Act of 2003 defines a child as anyone under 18, makes hotel operators liable if they knowingly allow child prostitution, and sets life imprisonment for child trafficking by tourists. The trade adjusted. By 2017 the US trafficking report found that traffickers increasingly hosted child sex tourists in private houses outside the tourist areas, where it is harder to detect. No representative survey of online child sexual abuse exists for West and Central Africa, so any shift from hotels to the internet would not show up in the figures either.

For a novice, The Gambia shows that a law aimed at hotels can push abuse into private homes rather than end it. Pressure is also needed in the countries the tourists come from, so it is worth asking whether those countries prosecute their citizens for what they do abroad.

LBN.story:
In late 2011, in the Maameltein red-light district of Jounieh, north of Beirut, security forces raided a brothel called Chez Maurice and found a 17-year-old Syrian girl trapped inside. The brothel closed for about three months and then reopened. In March 2016 Lebanese forces raided it again, together with a second brothel, Silver-B, and freed as many as 75 Syrian women. Over a dozen people were charged with sex trafficking. One survivor told the Lebanese legal publication Legal Agenda that a trafficker had claimed he had 'bought the state'. Lebanon's police identified 87 trafficking victims that year, most of them from this case.

The women came from the war next door. The 2025 US trafficking report says criminal groups recruit Syrian refugee women and girls with false job offers and then exploit them in Lebanese brothels, and that Syrian children are held in bonded labour in the Beqaa valley, working to pay off a debt. Human Rights Watch said Syrian refugee women were at particular risk. Beyond these cases, there is no representative survey of online child sexual abuse anywhere in the Middle East and North Africa, so that kind of abuse in Lebanon is not counted.

For a novice, Lebanon shows how a raid can end with the same business back open within months. When a place where a child was found is allowed to reopen, ask who licensed it and whether anyone was charged the first time.
